title: Beyond the Bubble
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Terry Underwood recounts being recruited in 1989 to a state design team for the CLAS reading test and uses the story to examine California's history of large-scale assessment. He traces the move from multiple-choice CAP testing, through the teacher-driven direct writing assessment, to CLAS's attempt at performance and portfolio assessment, and on to STAR, the API and today's Common Core stopgap. His argument is that CLAS was killed not mainly by parental complaints about privacy and content but because it could not produce the individual student scores that the testing regime had made sacred. He contrasts assessment built by teachers for instructional use with standardized tests sold as curriculum-neutral yet powerful enough to pull instruction toward themselves. The essay also introduces Judith Langer's envisionment-building theory as the basis of the CLAS reading design. Underwood ends by suggesting that a system without a coherent center, as exposed by COVID, is the consequence of the factory metaphor that authentic assessment might have challenged.
points: CLAS was defeated because it could not deliver individual achievement scores, the one thing the testing regime would not give up, rather than chiefly because of parental objections.
The WYTIWYG principle (what you test is what you get) frames assessment as a curriculum lever: if it is worth testing, it is worth teaching.
Standardized tests were marketed as curriculum-neutral, yet they drew instruction toward themselves like iron filings to magnets.
The API and zip-code comparison bands baked the Matthew Effect into accountability, pitting high-poverty schools against one another.
Assessment designed by teachers, for teachers, as evidence of learning opportunities is offered as the alternative to surveillance-style testing.
quotes: Enter a fine-tuned writing assessment program with eight genres of writing, banks of field tested writing prompts, and genre specific scoring rubrics. The CAP Direct Writing Assessment brought unprecedented coherence, the devilish angel, to teaching and learning writing.

It’s true that parents resisted CLAS with charges of invasion of privacy, indecent and controversial passages, and the like. But it was really about going beyond the bubble. It was honoring the bubble that ended it.
Gone were the days helping districts improve. Instead school test scores would arouse parents. Bad schools would be reconstituted.
CLAS was a full out effort to put teachers in the driver seat of school evaluation with professional accountability. Without robust political and economic support, CLAS would never work.

The idea was to create evidence of learning for teachers to use as collaborators and co-creators of a powerful lived curriculum—a measure of how well intentional student opportunities to learn were working. Such an assessment would be made for teachers by teachers and examined by teachers as a foundation for coherent and purposeful instruction.
WYTIWYG was the CLAS mantra: What You Test Is What You Get. If it’s important enough to test, it’s important enough to teach.

These tests were billed as curriculum-neutral, unbiased toward any particular pedagogy or textbook series. They had an uncanny force, however, that drew curriculum and instruction to them like iron filings to magnets.
